catalog_quote: Le zbu fait partie des langues tonales du type word-tone, « africain » ... le zbu et les autres langues rgyalrongs tonales se distinguent par l’importance d’une position accentuée avec les corrélats usuels d’un accent dynamique (stress). ... §38 Schémas tono-accentuels. Le mot prosodique minimum comporte une seule syllabe accentuée. L’accentuation se trouve soit sur la dernière syllabe, soit sur l’avant-dernière syllabe. Un mot prosodique accentué sur sa dernière syllabe admet une distinction de ton: le ton est soit plat, soit tombant. Aucune distinction de ton n’existe pour les mots accentués sur l’avant-dernière syllabe. Ceci nous donne trois cas possibles, qui portent, dans cette étude, des noms tirés des grammairiens grecs: • L’oxyton: σσσ́ʔ, accent final, ton plat. • Le périspomène: σσσ̂, accent final, ton tombant. • Le paroxyton: σσ́σ, accent pénultième.

new_statements.translation: §38 Tono-accentual patterns. The minimal prosodic word has a single accented syllable. The accent falls either on the last syllable or on the penultimate syllable. A prosodic word accented on its last syllable admits a tone distinction: the tone is either level or falling. No tone distinction exists for words accented on the penultimate syllable. This gives three possible cases, named in this study after the Greek grammarians: oxytone σσσ́ʔ, final accent, level tone; perispomenon σσσ̂, final accent, falling tone; paroxytone σσ́σ, penultimate accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Zbu (Rgyaltsu / Zbu A) is described as a word-tone language of the 'African' type in which every minimal prosodic word has exactly one accented syllable with stress-like correlates (intensity, duration, F0); the accent is restricted to a two-syllable final window (final or penultimate) and its position is lexically specified for nouns and lexically/morphologically determined for verbs (static oxytone/perispomenon/paroxytone stems vs kinetic stems that alternate final~penult depending on 'inert' vs 'retracting' prefixes). Final-accented words additionally contrast level (with glottal constriction) vs falling tone; penult-accented words carry no tone contrast. Author explicitly declines the label 'pitch accent' (following Hyman 2009).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; syllables preceding the accented one show a slight F0 rise or stay flat (p. 77). The prosodic word is recursive (compounds contain several minimal prosodic words), with compound accent mostly determined by the second member (§41) and processes of 'recul anastrophique' (§42) and 'cémise' (loss of final H of an oxytone inside an intonational group, §44).
new_statements.exceptions: Verbal suffixes (except -ŋ 1sg) are enclitics outside the minimal prosodic word and never shift the accent (§40). Dynamic-stress correlates are asymmetric: barely perceptible for final accent, strongly marked for penult accent (final unaccented syllable much shorter/weaker, often breathy or devoiced) (p. 77-79). Reduplication can yield proparoxytones exceeding the minimal-word window (p. 73-74). Compound accentuation has irregular/fluctuating cases (§41). Dialect split (p. 9): 'les parlers du zbu A sont des langues tonales, avec des systèmes tono-accentuels complexes; les parlers du zbu B, en revanche, sont des langues non tonales avec un système de pur accent dynamique (stress)' — Zbu B (Dzamgo) distinguishes only final vs penultimate stress (p. 17: 'On distingue l’accent final tə-χpûm « genou » et l’accent pénultième tɑ́-sɑʶ « sang »').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of the accent rule is the minimal prosodic word (conjugated verb without suffixes; morphologically simple noun); laryngeal and tonal correlates described chiefly for forms in pausa (citation forms); phrase-level 'cémise' can delete the final H of oxytones inside an intonational group. Description based on the Rgyaltsu (Ngyaltsu) village variety of Lower Zbu (Zbu A).
new_statements.identity_note: Gong 2018 describes the Rgyaltsu (Ngyaltsu) village variety of Lower Zbu ('zbu A'), Glottolog zbua1234 (Zbu; also called Showu 日部/Ribu rGyalrong in Sun 2004). The author notes a deep internal split: Zbu A dialects (Smar-chu/Rnga-chu valleys, incl. Rgyaltsu) are tonal with the accent+tone system quoted; Zbu B dialects (Rdo-chu valley, e.g. Dzamgo) are non-tonal with plain dynamic stress, final vs penultimate. No separate glottocodes exist for Zbu A/B.

tone_statements.quote: The Caodeng and Showu rGyalrong data cited here are from my years of fieldwork conducted in Sichuan. ... Transcription of the data is phonemic, using symbols roughly in their usual IPA values. Suprasegmental notations used are: | (pitch accent), — (level tone) and » (falling tone). See J. Sun (2003) for an overview of Caodeng rGyalrong phonology. ... [fn. 2:] The Sidaba dialect in turn subdivides into two distinct sub-dialects, Caodeng and Showu.

tone_statements.summary: Transcription distinguishes an accented syllable (pitch accent) and, on it, level vs falling tone - a three-way tono-accentual notation applied jointly to Caodeng and Showu (Zbu) forms; nothing further on tone-bearing unit, stress or rules for Showu in this paper (consistent with Gong 2018's oxytone / perispomenon / paroxytone analysis listed here).

sources.note: A Chinese-language PhD dissertation (Nankai, 2025) on the morphosyntax of the Marong (玛荣) dialect of Ribu = Zbu Rgyalrong; Jacques cites it (with Sun 2000, Gong 2018, Zhang 2020) as one of the reference descriptions of the four Core Gyalrong languages. Its treatment of tone/accent is unverified: a phonology overview with a 声调/重音 section is conventional in such theses but nothing of the text could be seen; if Marong lies in the Smar-chu/Rnga-chu basin (Zbu A) the variety is tonal per Gong 2018: 9, if in the Rdo-chu basin (Zbu B) it would be a pure stress variety - location not verified.
